name: Representable view
first: A SwiftUI view that makes and updates a UIKit view, so that a UIKit view can be used among SwiftUI views.

dependsOn.why: The example shows its view in a hosting controller, which lays it out without a window.
dependsOn.whyInExample: The constant `host` is a hosting controller, as `host` is on the page of Hosting controller.

dependsOn.why: A representable view is a SwiftUI view, which is placed among other views as any view is.
dependsOn.whyInExample: The view `CityLabel` can be placed among views, as `Greeting` can.

dependsOn.why: A UIKit view is an instance of a class, which SwiftUI keeps and changes by reference.
dependsOn.whyInExample: The call `UILabel()` makes an instance of a class, as `Counter()` does on the page of Class.

what.is: A representable view is a type that conforms to `UIViewRepresentable`. It is a SwiftUI view that shows a UIKit view: its method `makeUIView` makes the UIKit view once, and its method `updateUIView` changes it to match the SwiftUI view's values, each time they change.
what.afterExample: The view `CityLabel` shows a city in a UIKit label. SwiftUI makes the label once, and then sets its text from `city`. The program runs on an iPhone in the simulator, because UIKit is a framework of iOS.
what.problem: Some views exist only in UIKit, or in a library written for UIKit, such as a map with features that SwiftUI lacks. Writing them again in SwiftUI can be a lot of work. A representable view puts the UIKit view among SwiftUI views as it is.
what.how: Apple's documentation says that SwiftUI calls the methods of a representable view at the right times to make and update its view, and that the UIKit view does not tell SwiftUI about its own changes: for that, a coordinator, an object of the representable view's own, forwards its messages.

when.text: Use it for a UIKit view that SwiftUI has no match for, such as a view from a library written for UIKit.
Don't use it for a view that SwiftUI already has, such as a label or a button. The SwiftUI view is simpler, and updates with no code of yours.

parts.name: The conformance to `UIViewRepresentable`, line 4
parts.text: The colon and the name `UIViewRepresentable` after `CityLabel` say that it conforms to the protocol, which requires the methods `makeUIView` and `updateUIView`. With them, a `CityLabel` is a SwiftUI view.

parts.name: The method `makeUIView`, lines 6 to 9
parts.text: The method makes the UIKit view, a `UILabel`, and returns it. SwiftUI calls it once, when the view first appears, and keeps the label it returns.

parts.name: The method `updateUIView`, lines 10 to 15
parts.text: The method gets the label that SwiftUI kept, and changes it to match the values of `CityLabel`: line 14 sets its text to `city`. SwiftUI calls it after `makeUIView`, and again each time the values change.

steps.text: Lines 18 to 20 make a hosting controller whose root view is a `CityLabel` for Lima.
Line 22 asks the controller what size it needs inside 300 by 300 points. To lay out `CityLabel`, SwiftUI first calls `makeUIView`, and line 7 prints {{makeUIView}}.
SwiftUI then calls `updateUIView` with the label, and line 13 prints {{updateUIView: Lima}}. Line 14 sets the label's text to Lima.
The label has its text, so it has a size, and line 22 prints whether its width is more than zero: {{true}}.

end.text: SwiftUI made the UIKit label once, and then set it from the values of `CityLabel`, so the label showed among SwiftUI views.
